title: Why being insured does not mean being fully protected
summary: Abhishek Bansal, CEO, Insurance Business, InsuranceDekho, explains why understanding policy exclusions, co-payments, waiting periods and claim conditions is essential to assessing whether a health insurance plan offers adequate financial protection.
thbAction: Map the news to THB's provider CRM for referral growth, patient lifecycle engagement, and multi-facility relationship management across hospital and provider networks.
contentHtml:
A medical emergency rarely begins as a neat financial event. It starts with symptoms, hurried calls and the search for a hospital bed. Somewhere in between, a relative is asked for an insurance card or admission deposit. That is often the first time a policy bought years earlier is tested against a hospital bill rather than a brochure.

The 2025 Survey on Household Social Consumption: Health found that 47.4 per cent of people in rural India and 44.3 per cent in urban India were covered under a health insurance or financing scheme. Yet it recorded average out-of-pocket medical expenditure of ₹34,064 per hospitalisation, excluding childbirth, rising to ₹50,508 in private hospitals. The gap between being covered and adequately protected is where family savings come under pressure.

Start with the possible bill, not the premium

Many buyers begin by asking whether ₹5 lakh or ₹10 lakh is sufficient. There is no universal figure. The answer depends on where the family lives, the hospitals it is likely to use, the ages and medical histories of its members, and the household’s ability to absorb an uncovered expense.

Employer-provided insurance is useful, but it should not be the family’s only calculation. The cover may be modest; protection is linked to the job. Before treating it as a complete solution, check the coverage limit, who is covered and what happens when employment changes. For older parents, a separate assessment may make more sense than a family floater, where a single shared sum insured could be exhausted by a major claim.

A top-up or super top-up can provide additional protection after a deductible is crossed. In many policies, a top-up applies the deductible to each claim, while a super top-up may consider eligible claims together over the policy year.

Look beyond the sum insured

A policy can carry an impressive headline number and still leave the customer with a meaningful share of the bill. Room-rent limits, co-payments, sub-limits, deductibles and exclusions affect what is payable. Waiting periods decide when cover begins for conditions, while rules on consumables and non-medical items can create out-of-pocket costs.

Consider a hypothetical ₹10 lakh policy against a ₹12 lakh hospital bill. A co-payment, room-rent limit, deductible or non-payable item can increase the family’s out-of-pocket share. The headline sum insured alone does not describe the family’s exposure.

This is why the most useful question is not simply, “What is my sum insured?” It is, “In a realistic claim, what might my family still have to pay?”

Price is often the opening question. It should not be the final one. Two plans with similar premiums may behave differently during hospitalisation. A comparison should examine the room category, co-payment, waiting periods, exclusions, pre- and post-hospitalisation cover, restoration benefit and cashless hospital network.

The IRDAI Annual Report 2024–25 says general and health insurers settled 3.26 crore claims, paying ₹94,248 crore. It recorded 87 per cent as settled, around 8 per cent as repudiated and about 5 per cent as pending at year end. That is not a judgement on an individual claim; it underlines the value of understanding policy conditions.

Make sure the policy can be used where you need it

Cashless treatment can reduce the need to arrange a large amount immediately, but only if the hospital and claim process work for the family. Check whether preferred hospitals are in the network. Also understand whom to contact, what documents are required and how an emergency admission must be reported.

Restoration benefits are not uniform. Some restore the sum insured only after it is exhausted; others may have conditions involving the same illness or the same family member. The word “restoration” is not enough; the trigger matters.

Accurate disclosure is equally important. Existing illnesses, medication and relevant medical history should be stated correctly in the proposal form. Clear disclosure can prevent avoidable uncertainty when the policy is needed.

 Review the cover before a crisis does it for you

Health insurance should not be bought once and forgotten. Marriage, childbirth, ageing parents, relocation, a new diagnosis, a change of job, income or financial obligations can alter a family’s needs. An annual review helps identify whether the sum insured, network access and policy features still match the family’s circumstances.

Hospitalisation is only one part of healthcare expenditure. Consultations, diagnostics, medicines and ongoing management of chronic conditions can create costs and may not be covered in the same way as an in-patient claim.

Preparation includes small practical steps: keep the e-card and helpline details accessible, ensure another family member knows the policy. At renewal, a family should identify its shared or individual cover, room-rent, co-payment and waiting-period conditions, cashless hospital access and the financial gap it may still need to fund.

The real measure of adequate health insurance is not the size of the policy on paper. It is the financial gap a family must bridge when treatment cannot wait. The right cover protects more than a hospital bill; it protects the savings meant for a child’s education, a home or retirement. Being insured and being adequately financially protected are not always the same thing.
